paragraphs: Determinantal point processes describe collections of points that tend to repel one another. This makes them useful for selecting diverse outcomes. For a finite list of candidates, an efficient sampling method uses an eigendecomposition of the kernel matrix. The paper addresses the harder situation in which possible points occupy a continuous space instead.

The discrete sampling procedure has a formal continuous counterpart, but its computational steps are directly usable only in restricted cases. The authors develop approximate sampling methods using Nyström approximations and random Fourier features. These provide practical ways to work with continuous DPPs across a broad range of kernel functions.

The paper demonstrates the methods in repulsive mixture modeling and in generating human poses that span activity spaces. These applications illustrate why continuous diversity matters: the desired outputs need not come from a predefined finite collection. The contribution is an efficient approximate route to sampling such collections, extending the practical reach of DPP modeling beyond discrete candidate selection.
neurips-2013-approximate-inference-in-co.tldr: Approximate sampling methods make continuous determinantal point processes practical for modeling diverse collections of points.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives contain losses or penalties with sharp corners, making optimization difficult. A common response is to replace these nonsmooth functions with smooth approximations. This paper revisits that choice and develops an approximation that remains nonsmooth while still supporting an efficient optimization algorithm.

The construction acts as though the proximal map has a linearity property. Rather than leaving this as an unsupported computational shortcut, the authors justify the resulting approximation through the proximal average, a tool from convex analysis. This supplies the mathematical basis for a new proximal gradient algorithm.

The paper establishes that its algorithm is strictly better than the smoothing-based algorithm in the comparison studied, without additional computational overhead. Experiments on overlapping group lasso and graph-guided fused lasso support the theoretical claims. Both applications involve penalties whose structure creates optimization challenges. The result shows that smoothing is not the only productive way to simplify these problems: a carefully justified nonsmooth approximation can yield a better algorithm without making each computational step more expensive.
neurips-2013-better-approximation-and-fa.tldr: A proximal-average approximation yields a proximal gradient algorithm with better theoretical performance than the studied smoothing approach at no extra overhead.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer causal relationships from observational time series. Its TiMINo models require the residual time series—the parts left unexplained by the model—to be independent. This differs from traditional Granger-style methods, which use residual variance to assess predictive relationships.

Restricting the structural equations, for example to additive-noise models, enables broader identifiability results. The theory covers nonlinear effects, both immediate and delayed relationships, certain unfaithful cases, and feedback that operates through time rather than instantaneously. These results establish conditions under which causal structure can be distinguished from observational data.

The practical algorithm has a narrower scope: it assumes no feedback loops between time series and uses nonlinear independence tests. When relevant causes are missing or model assumptions fail, it may return partial results and mostly avoids incorrect answers; this is not a guarantee of correctness under misspecification. The framework also accommodates different measurement delays across series. Experiments on artificial and real data report better performance than existing methods, supporting the usefulness of the independence-based approach.
neurips-2013-causal-inference-on-time-se.tldr: TiMINo uses independent residual time series and restricted structural equations to identify causal relationships under stated model conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies several players collaborating to find a nearly best option in a multi-armed bandit problem. Each player can gather evidence by pulling arms, and the shared target is an arm within epsilon of optimal. The question is how much parallel exploration helps when communication is limited.

With k players and only one opportunity to communicate, the authors establish a square-root-of-k speedup relative to one player. A matching lower bound shows that this is generally the best possible improvement under that communication restriction. Having more players therefore does not automatically produce a proportional reduction in each player's exploration burden.

With additional communication, the paper gives an algorithm that reaches the ideal factor-k speedup. Its communication requirement grows only logarithmically with inverse epsilon. Together, the results describe a concrete tradeoff between gathering more observations locally and exchanging information across players. This matters for computationally intensive applications because distributing work and coordinating that work are separate resources, and the available coordination changes the achievable benefit of parallel learning.
neurips-2013-distributed-exploration-in-.tldr: Collaborating bandit players achieve a square-root-of-k speedup with one communication round and a factor-k speedup with more communication.

paragraphs: Clustering sequential batches of data becomes difficult when groups evolve and their number is unknown. The paper develops an algorithm for this setting from the dependent Dirichlet process mixture model. Its aim is to retain a model of changing clusters while making the actual clustering computation substantially faster.

The authors derive the procedure by examining the low-variance limit of a Gibbs sampling algorithm for that model. The resulting method produces hard assignments, placing observations into individual clusters. It also has convergence guarantees resembling those of k-means, connecting a probabilistic model of evolving groups to a simpler clustering procedure.

Evaluation uses moving Gaussian clusters in synthetic data and real aircraft trajectories recorded through ADS-B. On those datasets, the method takes orders of magnitude less computation time than the contemporary probabilistic and hard clustering methods considered, while also achieving higher accuracy. These findings support the value of the asymptotic derivation for the tested dynamic clustering problems. The reported speed and accuracy advantages are empirical results on those datasets, rather than universal performance guarantees.
neurips-2013-dynamic-clustering-via-asym.tldr: A low-variance derivation turns a dependent mixture model into an efficient hard-clustering algorithm for unknown numbers of evolving groups.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to make Gaussian process regression more manageable by selecting a subset of training observations. This subset serves as the inducing set that creates a sparse model. The central computational task is deciding which observations to retain while also fitting the model's hyperparameters.

The proposed discrete optimization algorithm handles both decisions through one objective. That objective can be either marginal likelihood or variational free energy. Using a common criterion connects the choice of inducing observations to the fitting of the model, rather than treating subset selection as an unrelated preliminary decision.

The algorithm's time and memory requirements grow linearly with training-set size, making it applicable to large regression problems. It supports both discrete and continuous domains, although the inducing set itself is selected from training data. Empirical evaluation reports state-of-the-art performance in the discrete setting and competitive results in the continuous setting. The findings support a scalable subset-selection approach while distinguishing the stronger reported comparative result for discrete problems from the more qualified result for continuous ones.
neurips-2013-efficient-optimization-for-.tldr: A discrete optimization method jointly selects inducing observations and fits sparse Gaussian process hyperparameters with linear scaling in training-set size.

paragraphs: A sample can leave many possible outcomes unseen, yet still contain enough information to estimate properties of the underlying distribution. The paper builds on results showing that entropy, distinct-element counts, and certain distribution distances can be estimated from independent samples of size O(n/log n) for distributions over at most n elements.

Its modification focuses on reconstructing the shape of the unseen portion of the distribution. Estimating only the total probability assigned to unobserved outcomes does not describe how that probability is distributed among them. The proposed approach seeks this richer characterization as a basis for estimating distributional properties.

The authors prove that their estimator is optimal up to constant factors on worst-case instances. They also report strong practical performance across multiple estimation tasks, natural distributions, and parameter settings. The theoretical result concerns worst-case efficiency, while the experiments show usefulness across the tested conditions. The authors further suggest that estimating unseen structure could become a component of larger learning and analysis systems; this is presented as a potential application.
neurips-2013-estimating-the-unseen-impro.tldr: Estimating the shape of unobserved probability mass yields property estimators that are worst-case optimal up to constants and perform strongly in experiments.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks independent components within observed data, but standard algorithms deteriorate when Gaussian noise is added. The paper identifies ordinary whitening as part of the problem: applying PCA and rescaling to identity covariance does not preserve invariance to that noise.

The authors develop a more efficient noise-invariant decorrelation procedure using Hessians of cumulant functions. They combine this with GI-ICA, a simple fixed-point algorithm based on a special gradient iteration. This iteration differs from gradient descent and works with the proposed quasi-orthogonalization procedure, as well as ordinary PCA whitening in the noiseless case.

The paper provides a convergence analysis based on properties of cumulants and presents the combined approach as a practical ICA algorithm with provable Gaussian-noise invariance. Experiments report superior results on noisy observations and very competitive results without noise. The contribution therefore addresses both the preprocessing step and the component-finding iteration, showing how a theoretically appropriate treatment of Gaussian noise can be incorporated into an efficient procedure with favorable empirical performance.
neurips-2013-fast-algorithms-for-gaussia.tldr: Noise-invariant decorrelation and a fast fixed-point iteration provide practical independent component analysis with provable Gaussian-noise invariance.

paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders learn to reconstruct data after corruption. Earlier work connected this training to the distribution that generated the data, but the established connection relied on continuous variables, Gaussian corruption, and squared reconstruction error. Its mathematical justification also depended on corruption becoming very small.

The paper proposes a different treatment that broadens the connection between reconstruction training and generative modeling. It handles discrete as well as continuous variables and allows other corruption processes, provided they are noisy enough. Reconstruction losses are interpreted as log-likelihoods, supplying a probabilistic meaning for the reconstruction objective.

The approach also removes the bias associated with corruption that is not infinitesimal, or with a contractive penalty that is not infinitesimal. This matters because the theory then reaches beyond the small-noise limiting case that constrained earlier justifications. The contribution is a more general account of how these reconstruction-based models estimate a data distribution, with explicit qualifications on corruption and loss interpretation. The abstract presents this as a methodological and mathematical extension rather than an empirical comparison.
neurips-2013-generalized-denoising-auto-.tldr: The paper broadens the generative interpretation of denoising autoencoders to discrete data, more corruption processes, and finite corruption levels.

paragraphs: Policy iteration improves a decision policy until it reaches an optimal discounted policy in a Markov decision process. The paper studies two versions: Howard's method updates every state with positive advantage, whereas Simplex-PI updates only the state with the largest advantage. Its focus is the number of iterations required.

For n states, m actions per state, and discount factor gamma, the authors sharpen existing bounds for both methods by a logarithmic factor in n. Their bounds scale respectively as nm and n²m, multiplied by a shared term involving 1/(1−gamma) and its logarithm. These are upper bounds on iteration counts, not reported runtime measurements.

The paper also obtains discount-independent bounds under structural assumptions involving transient duration and return times to recurrent states across policies. One result applies to Simplex-PI and generalizes a deterministic-MDP result. A stronger, explicitly restrictive assumption fixes which states are transient or recurrent under every policy and enables bounds for both variants. Thus, additional structural information can replace discount dependence, but the applicable assumptions differ across the results.
neurips-2013-improved-and-generalized-up.tldr: Sharper iteration bounds improve guarantees for two policy-iteration variants, with discount-independent results under additional structural assumptions.

paragraphs: Multi-task prediction shares information among related prediction problems. The paper highlights a common assumption that can interfere with this goal: task outputs are treated as independent once the inputs are accounted for. Correlations can still remain in the residuals, the portions of outputs that the regressors do not explain.

The proposed Gaussian process model represents both relationships among regressors and correlations among residuals. Modeling these two sources of dependence is intended to identify more accurately which information should genuinely be shared between regressors. Shared unexplained variation therefore receives its own place in the model.

The resulting covariance is expressed as a sum of Kronecker products, with efficient parameter inference and prediction on new observations remaining feasible. Experiments on synthetic examples and genetic phenotype prediction show substantial benefits over established alternatives. These findings support the practical importance of modeling structured noise in the evaluated settings. The methodological contribution is to combine a richer account of cross-task dependence with computations that still allow the model to be fitted and used for prediction.
neurips-2013-it-is-all-in-the-noise-effi.tldr: A multi-task Gaussian process models both shared regressors and correlated residuals, improving prediction in synthetic and genetics applications.

paragraphs: The paper tackles sparse precision matrix estimation in high dimensions using the CLIME estimator. Its contribution centers on making this estimation computationally manageable at very large scales. The authors introduce an inexact alternating direction method of multipliers and establish convergence rates for both the objective and the optimality conditions.

The distributed framework divides the CLIME computation into blocks of columns. Its core operations are elementwise calculations and parallel matrix multiplications, allowing work to be spread across processors. The implementation also supports block-cyclic data and parameter distribution to balance workloads and improve use of memory hierarchies.

The authors evaluate the approach on shared-memory and distributed-memory architectures. They report computations reaching millions of dimensions and trillions of parameters using hundreds of cores, with substantially better scalability than the comparison methods. Scaling is almost linear in core count in the experiments. The result combines an optimization algorithm with a distribution strategy suited to large matrices, showing that the organization of computation can substantially expand the practical scale of an existing statistically motivated estimator.
neurips-2013-large-scale-distributed-spa.tldr: An inexact ADMM algorithm and distributed column-block computation make CLIME precision estimation scalable to extremely large matrices.

paragraphs: Optical flow describes local image motion. The paper uses datasets with known flow to learn how small flow patterns are distributed, then compares the learned description with models commonly assumed by optical-flow algorithms. This directly examines whether those modeling assumptions match observed local motion statistics.

A Gaussian mixture with 64 components provides a significantly better statistical model than the commonly used alternatives considered. The authors investigate why it succeeds and connect its advantage to explicitly representing flow boundaries. Accounting for places where motion changes is therefore central to the reported improvement.

The paper also learns a joint model of local image intensity and flow. It finds that motion boundaries are more likely near intensity boundaries, consistent with a common computer-vision assumption. However, the dependence is very weak on a large dataset, and conditioning flow estimation on local intensity offers only marginal benefit. The findings distinguish two issues: representing motion boundaries improves the flow model, while nearby intensity patterns provide relatively little additional information in the evaluated local setting.
neurips-2013-learning-the-local-statisti.tldr: A 64-component Gaussian mixture better captures local flow statistics, while local intensity patterns offer only marginal additional benefit.

paragraphs: The paper studies probability estimation when individual data must remain private even from the statistician carrying out the analysis. It considers both discrete and continuous distributions. This places privacy inside the estimation problem itself, because the analyst cannot simply work with unrestricted observations.

The authors establish sharp minimax convergence rates for this setting. These rates characterize the best worst-case estimation performance under the privacy constraints. They expose a fundamental relationship between privacy and statistical efficiency: the privacy requirement affects how quickly an estimated distribution can approach the underlying one as evidence accumulates.

The work also supplies tools for choosing positions along that privacy-efficiency tradeoff. A concrete consequence concerns Warner's randomized response method for surveys, which the analysis identifies as optimal for maintaining respondent privacy in the studied setting. This connects an established survey technique to a broader theory of private probability estimation. The significance is both a performance benchmark for locally private procedures and a principled account of how privacy choices relate to the accuracy those procedures can attain.
neurips-2013-local-privacy-and-minimax-b.tldr: Sharp minimax bounds characterize privacy–accuracy tradeoffs in locally private distribution estimation and establish optimality of randomized response in the studied survey setting.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately two Gaussian populations can be separated when observations have many dimensions and the population means are close. It studies a mixture of two isotropic Gaussians, a specific setting in which the authors can derive precise statistical limits for clustering.

The main results give information-theoretic bounds on clustering accuracy and the amount of data needed. These bounds address what the observations make possible, rather than only analyzing the behavior of a particular implementation. Small mean separation is central to the setting because the two populations are difficult to distinguish.

When only a sparse subset of dimensions determines the difference between the means, the stated sample complexity depends on the number of relevant dimensions and the separation. A simple, computationally efficient procedure attains this dependence. The sparsity condition therefore connects a statistical advantage to an achievable algorithm. The authors present the results as an initial theoretical foundation for methods that combine feature selection with clustering, showing why focusing on the dimensions that separate groups can matter.
neurips-2013-minimax-theory-for-high-dim.tldr: For two weakly separated isotropic Gaussians, sparse mean separation enables sample complexity governed by relevant dimensions and attainable by an efficient procedure.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning a new visual category from a single image. Its hierarchical Bayesian model combines compositionality, which represents concepts through parts, with causality, which concerns how an image is produced. Learning is framed around recovering that structured process from the observed example.

This approach allows the model to generalize across a range of natural but simple visual concepts. The emphasis on a process behind the image supports more than assigning a class label: the same conceptual representation can also be assessed through generating examples and parsing visual structure.

On a challenging one-shot classification task, the model achieves an error rate comparable to humans and substantially outperforms two deep learning models. A visual Turing test also finds human-like performance on generation and parsing tasks. These are results for the evaluated tasks and the paper's relatively simple visual concepts. Together, they show that a compositional, causal Bayesian representation can support several forms of generalization from one observation, rather than requiring separate evidence for each conceptual task.
neurips-2013-one-shot-learning-by-invert.tldr: A compositional causal Bayesian model learns simple visual concepts from one image and achieves human-level error on the evaluated classification task.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decision-making when an adversary chooses both losses and state-transition distributions. Under a mixing assumption, its algorithm achieves regret O(√(T log|Π|) + log|Π|) against a comparison set of policies Π. This bound does not depend on the sizes of the state and action spaces.

Computational efficiency requires additional conditions: expectations over trajectories must be efficiently computable, and the policy comparison set must have polynomial size. The authors also examine an episodic shortest-path problem, where each episode supplies a directed acyclic graph and edge losses are revealed after the path is traversed.

Efficient solutions are available when graphs are random and losses adversarial, or when graphs are adversarial and losses random. When both are adversarial, the proposed efficient algorithm has regret growing linearly with the number of distinct graphs. Finally, a hardness result connects efficient algorithms for the general adversarial problem to learning parity with noise. The results therefore separate favorable regret guarantees from the additional conditions needed to achieve them efficiently.
neurips-2013-online-learning-in-markov-d.tldr: Adversarial MDP learning admits state-space-independent regret under mixing, while efficient computation depends on additional conditions and faces a hardness barrier.

paragraphs: Bayesian online change-point detection tracks when the parameters generating a sequence may have changed abruptly. Its computation relies on posterior predictive distributions from the underlying model. The paper addresses cases outside the exponential family where these predictions are intractable and the usual constant-time, constant-memory online predictive updates are unavailable.

The authors develop variational approximations to the distribution over change-point times, expressed through run lengths. A run length describes how long the current segment has lasted since a change. Approximating this uncertainty enables efficient inference when the underlying observation model does not support the usual tractable calculations.

The work also improves online variational inference and applies the resulting methodology to radar tracking. In that application, a signal-to-noise feature follows a Rice distribution. The authors develop a variational method for estimating the parameters of that non-exponential-family distribution as well. The contribution joins approximate change-point tracking with approximate inference for the observation model, extending the kinds of data-generating distributions that can be handled by the online change-detection framework.
neurips-2013-online-variational-approxim.tldr: Variational approximations extend online Bayesian change-point inference to intractable non-exponential-family models, including a Rice-distributed radar feature.

paragraphs: Ordinary multi-task learning considers related tasks together. This paper introduces parametric task learning, where a continuous parameter indexes an entire family of tasks. The formulation can therefore represent infinitely many related tasks without treating them as an individually enumerated collection.

The key finding applies to a particular class of these problems: the optimal solution for each task traces a piecewise-linear path as the task parameter varies. Within each piece, the solution changes linearly with that parameter. The authors use this structure through parametric programming to obtain a common representation shared across the continuous task family efficiently.

The paper illustrates the formulation in learning under non-stationarity, cost-sensitive learning, and quantile regression, and reports experiments supporting its usefulness in those scenarios. These examples show why a continuum of tasks can be a useful modeling choice when the learning problem changes with a parameter. The efficiency argument rests on the piecewise-linear result for the specified class of problems; the abstract does not claim that every continuously parameterized task family has this structure.
neurips-2013-parametric-task-learning-f4.tldr: Parametric task learning efficiently shares representations across certain continuous task families by exploiting piecewise-linear paths of optimal solutions.

paragraphs: The paper considers an agent that solves a sequence of Markov decision processes during a finite lifetime. Because the agent has computational limits, the reward that specifies a task need not be the most helpful reward for guiding its behavior. Earlier work motivates using alternative guidance rewards to compensate for those limits.

The proposed transfer method reuses successful guidance rewards from previous tasks. As experience accumulates, the agent trains a mapping from task-specifying reward functions to initial guidance reward functions. For a subsequent task, this mapping supplies a starting form of guidance informed by earlier problems.

This shifts the transferred knowledge toward how the agent should be encouraged to behave. The paper demonstrates that the approach can substantially improve performance relative to other transfer approaches, including one that transfers policies. The claim is a demonstrated potential improvement for bounded agents in the studied sequential-task setting. Its broader significance is that useful experience can be captured in a learned relationship between a task's stated objective and the reward that helps a computationally limited agent pursue it.
neurips-2013-reward-mapping-for-transfer.tldr: Learning a mapping from task rewards to guidance rewards lets computationally bounded agents transfer useful experience across successive tasks.

paragraphs: RNADE estimates a joint probability density for vectors of real-valued observations. It constructs that density as a product of one-dimensional conditional densities. This breaks a multidimensional estimation problem into linked predictions for individual coordinates while preserving an explicit expression for the density of a complete observation.

Each conditional is modeled with a mixture density network, and the networks share parameters. The model also learns a distributed representation of the data. The central combination is a learned neural representation together with density calculations that remain tractable.

A tractable likelihood permits training with standard gradient-based optimizers and direct likelihood comparisons with other density estimators. The paper evaluates RNADE on several datasets covering heterogeneous and perceptual data. It outperforms mixture models in all but one of the evaluated cases. That exception preserves the empirical scope of the finding: RNADE performs better across most of these comparisons, without establishing a universal advantage. The work shows how neural conditional models can be assembled into a practical joint density estimator.
neurips-2013-rnade-the-real-valued-neura.tldr: RNADE combines shared neural conditional density models into a tractable joint density estimator that beats mixture models on most tested datasets.

paragraphs: Large neural recordings may contain activity governed by a much smaller set of underlying dynamics. The paper develops a convex dimensionality-reduction method for finding this structure without strong assumptions about those dynamics or averaging over many trials. It extends the idea of PCA to exponential-family models through nuclear norm minimization.

The extracted structure can be combined with spectral methods to learn dynamical-system models. The authors assess fit using an exact decomposition of Bregman divergence that plays a role analogous to variance explained in PCA. This provides a way to evaluate the representation within the broader statistical setting.

On model data, the method recovers parameters of latent linear dynamical systems and can recover the true latent subspace even when dynamics are nonstationary. An extension separates sparse local connections from global latent dynamics. On monkey motor-cortex recordings, nuclear norm smoothing improves prediction compared with fitting linear dynamical models without that smoothing. These results support the method both as a way to extract low-dimensional structure and as preparation for learning predictive dynamics.
neurips-2013-robust-learning-of-low-dime.tldr: Convex nuclear norm smoothing extracts low-dimensional neural structure and improves dynamical prediction on the evaluated motor-cortex data.

paragraphs: Kernel embeddings provide a way to represent probability distributions for machine learning. This paper focuses on distributions with latent or low-rank structure, where a simpler underlying organization can be useful even when the observed distribution is multivariate. The authors argue that such structure had received little attention in kernel-embedding methods.

They propose a hierarchical low-rank decomposition of the embeddings. The approach is designed to exploit low-rank information while remaining robust when that information is misspecified. These two goals are linked: using a structural model is more useful when an inaccurate description of the latent structure does not undermine the representation.

The paper supplies empirical evidence that the estimated low-rank embeddings improve density estimation. This connects the proposed representation to a downstream statistical task, rather than assessing the decomposition only as an abstract construction. The stated contribution is a structure-aware and robust embedding method, with practical support from density-estimation experiments. The abstract reports improvement in those experiments without claiming that every distribution or every use of kernel embeddings benefits equally.
neurips-2013-robust-low-rank-kernel-embe.tldr: Hierarchical low-rank kernel embeddings exploit latent structure while addressing misspecification and improve density estimation in experiments.

paragraphs: Majorization-minimization optimizes an objective by repeatedly minimizing a surrogate that bounds it from above. The paper makes this principle scalable through a stochastic scheme that can handle very large or potentially infinite datasets. It turns a broad optimization strategy into a framework for learning from data at scale.

For convex objectives under suitable assumptions, the expected convergence rate is O(1/√n) after n iterations, improving to O(1/n) for strongly convex objectives. For a large class of nonconvex problems, the scheme converges almost surely to stationary points. That nonconvex conclusion concerns stationarity rather than a guarantee of reaching a global optimum.

The framework yields several algorithms. A stochastic proximal gradient method experimentally matches leading solvers for large-scale l1-regularized logistic regression. An online difference-of-convex programming method addresses nonconvex sparse estimation, and further experiments demonstrate effectiveness for structured matrix factorization. These applications show that the common surrogate-minimization principle supports multiple problem types while retaining convergence guarantees appropriate to their different mathematical settings.
neurips-2013-stochastic-majorization-min.tldr: Stochastic majorization-minimization scales surrogate-based optimization while providing conditional convex rates and nonconvex stationarity guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper introduces SDA-Bayes, a framework for estimating a Bayesian posterior as data arrive. Its design supports streaming data, distributed computation, and asynchronous operation. The posterior estimate is updated through an approximation function supplied by the user, making the framework broader than one particular approximation technique.

To demonstrate the idea, the authors choose variational Bayes as that approximation function and fit latent Dirichlet allocation to two large document collections. This gives a concrete test of the framework in a model for document collections while retaining the distinction between the general updating framework and the particular inference method used inside it.

The experiments show advantages over stochastic variational inference in a single-pass setting and also demonstrate the streaming setting, to which the compared SVI approach does not apply. The distinction matters because processing a collection once and supporting ongoing posterior updates are different operational requirements. The contribution is a framework that accommodates those ongoing updates and distributed asynchronous computation, supported by the reported large-scale document-modeling results.
neurips-2013-streaming-variational-bayes.tldr: SDA-Bayes supports streaming, distributed, asynchronous posterior approximation and demonstrates advantages with variational Bayes on large document collections.
